en: Preface to the Seventh Assembly of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
The Mañjuśrī Section,
composed by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xímíng Monastery.
I have heard that when one abides in appearances, there is nothing to be seen, thereby manifesting the magnificent vision of True Suchness;
when one abides in thought, there is no cognition, thereby perfecting the silent realization of the Knowledge of All Modes.
Yet, as long as the two types of dust remain, the temporal perceptions will fluctuate between lightness and density.
As the five veils are about to be dispelled, they may again gather or disperse due to doubt.
For this reason, the Way of Emptiness was suddenly clarified at the site where Anāthapiṇḍada gathered his followers;
and through the successive selection of worthy disciples, Śāriputra ascended to the solemnity of the public proclamation.

Suddenly there is nothing to behold in reverent gazing; in an instant there is nothing to hear for the nourishment of awakening. Having obliterated cultivation yet established cultivation, one likewise transcends learning yet hastens toward learning.
To delineate its distinctions, there are ten thousand streams of Bodhi;
to sever its chaotic confusion, there is the single mark of Nirvana.

In the single characteristic, one does not perceive birth and death; in the myriad streams, there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma. Without destroying the profusion of conventional designations, one opens up the vast emptiness of the true reality.
It is clearly demonstrated that even the dharmas of the Tathāgata do not exist, let alone the dharmas of bodhisattvas;
the dharmas of bodhisattvas do not exist, let alone the dharmas of the two vehicles;
the dharmas of the two vehicles do not exist, let alone the dharmas of ordinary beings.
If even dharmas do not exist, how can there be bodhi?
Since there is no bodhi, how can one proceed toward it?
Since there is nothing toward which to proceed, how can there be realization?
Since there is as yet no realization, how could there be one who realizes?

Therefore, where there is existence, there is distinction; where there is non-existence, there is penetration. Where there is clarity, there is vastness; where there is obstruction, there is limitation.

To be suddenly expansive and unimpeded yet without relaxation; to be fervently uplifted and diligent yet not yet perfected; to distinguish the blooming of compassion from the miasma of affliction; and to compare the forest of swords with the color of the jade-hair—these are all within his domain.
Why should these be changed?

Observe how they employ provisional verbal paths for ease of access and look up to the true principle for ultimate rest; like shimmering pearls rolling on and like the clear chimes of jade resonating, they give rise to the Sage’s intent—nothing surpasses this!
To bask one’s body in the light of the Dharma King is indeed most fitting!
Thus, to explore its meaning is to unlock the mysterious portal of the secret treasury;
to savor its discourse is to embrace the divergent paths of the esoteric teachings.
The phrasing is elegant and the meaning is profound; this is none other than the old *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Although it consists of two fascicles as a single work, its admonitions are fully manifest, providing a refuge for the seven classes of followers, clearly and without distance.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 574.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
The Seventh Part of the Mañjuśrī Section. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus numbering one hundred thousand, all of whom were arhats, with the sole exception of Ānanda, who still remained on the stage of a learner; Śāriputra and others served as their leaders.

Furthermore, he was accompanied by a multitude of ten thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were adorned with the armor of non-regressive merit; they were headed by the bodhisattvas Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, A-pratihata-pratibhāna, and A-tyakta-yoga.
When the first light of dawn appeared, the youth Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva emerged from his dwelling and went to where the Tathāgata was, standing outside.

At that same time, the venerable Śāriputra, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākauṣṭhila, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahānāman, and all such great śrāvaka monks likewise emerged from their respective dwellings, went to where the Tathāgata was, and stood outside.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the great assembly had all gathered, emerged from his dwelling and sat cross-legged upon his usual seat. He addressed Śāriputra:
"For what reason are you standing outside the gate at this early hour?"
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The youth Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva arrived here first; we arrived later.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "Good son!
Is it true that you have previously come to this dwelling place out of a desire to behold, pay homage to, and draw near to the Buddha?"
Mañjuśrī came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One! Why is this?"

I have never grown weary of beholding, paying homage to, and drawing near to the Tathāgata; it was for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings that I truly came here first.
World-Honored One!

My coming now to this place to draw near, pay homage, and behold the Tathāgata is solely for the purpose of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings; it is not for the sake of attaining the Buddha’s bodhi, nor for the sake of gazing upon the body of the Tathāgata, nor for the sake of disturbing the true dharma-realm, nor for the sake of discriminating the nature of phenomena, nor for the sake of any other various matters.

I contemplate the Tathāgata as the very nature of True Suchness (tathatā): unmoving and unconditioned; without conceptualization or discursive differentiation; neither identical with nor separate from spatial locations; neither existent nor non-existent; neither eternal nor annihilated; neither identical with nor separate from the three periods of time; without birth or cessation; without going or coming; unstained and not stained; neither dual nor non-dual—beyond the paths of mind and speech.

If one contemplates the Tathāgata through these characteristics of suchness, it is called truly seeing the Buddha; it is also called paying homage to and drawing near to the Tathāgata, which can truly bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī,
“In making this contemplation,
what do you see? Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!
When I contemplate in this way, I see nothing at all; regarding the characteristics of all phenomena, I likewise grasp at nothing.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent,
young man!”
"You are able to contemplate the Tathāgata in this way: regarding all phenomena, your mind neither grasps nor rejects anything; it neither accumulates nor disperses.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī, "It is truly rare that you are able to approach, pay homage to, and contemplate the Tathāgata in such a manner!"
Although he constantly regards all sentient beings with loving-kindness and compassion, he apprehends no sentient being at all;
although he is able to transform and guide all sentient beings toward nirvāṇa, he has no attachment;
although he dons the great armor for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, he does not give rise to any expedient means of accumulation or dispersal therein.
Then Mañjuśrī addressed Śāriputra, saying: “So it is! So it is!”

As the Honored One has taught, for the sake of the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, I don the great armor to lead them toward nirvāṇa; yet, in reality, regarding both sentient beings and the realm of nirvāṇa—whether as those to be transformed or as that which is realized—I have neither attainment nor grasping.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
it is not that I truly desire to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings that I don this great armor. Why is that?
The realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.

Suppose that within this single buddha-field there were as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and each one were to remain for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, constantly preaching as many Dharma-gates day and night, with each individual Dharma-gate being able to deliver as many sentient beings from those buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, causing them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
Just as such things occur in this buddha-field, so it is likewise in all other worlds throughout the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Although there are that many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who for that long a time teach that many dharmas and deliver that many sentient beings, causing them all to realize entry into nirvana without remainder, the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.
"Why is this? Because all sentient beings are by nature detached and have no limits; they cannot be increased or diminished.
Śāriputra said:

“Mañjuśrī! If all sentient beings, by their very nature, are free from [intrinsic existence], and because they are without limit, neither increase nor decrease, for what reason do bodhisattvas seek great enlightenment and desire to constantly preach the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?”
Mañjuśrī said: "Śāriputra! I say that sentient beings are entirely unapprehendable;
how then could there be a bodhisattva seeking great enlightenment who wishes to constantly preach the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?"
Why is this? Śāriputra,
because all phenomena are ultimately unapprehendable.
The Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
“If all sentient beings are entirely unapprehendable, how can a realm of sentient beings be established? Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!
The realm of sentient beings is merely a provisional designation. “Mañjuśrī!”
Suppose someone were to ask you:
"How many are there in the realm of sentient beings?
When you encounter such a question, how would you answer?
“World-Honored One!
I would answer thus:
‘As are the enumerations of the Buddha-dharmas, so too are those realms.’”
“Mañjuśrī! Suppose you were asked again:
‘What is the measure of the realm of sentient beings?’”
“If you were asked that question, how would you answer?
“World-Honored One,
I would answer in this way:”
"The extent of the realm of sentient beings is like the sphere of the Buddhas.
"Mañjuśrī, suppose someone were to ask: [what is the measure of the realm of sentient beings?]"
"To what does the realm of all sentient beings belong?
If you were asked this question, how would you answer?
"World-Honored One!"
"I shall answer thus:
'The realm to which that belongs is as inconceivable as the Buddha. "Mañjuśrī!"
Suppose someone were to ask:
"In what does the realm of sentient beings abide?
How would you answer such a question?
“World-Honored One!
I would answer thus:
‘The dharmas that should be dwelt in at the limit of detachment from passion are themselves the dharmas that should be dwelt in by the realm of sentient beings.’”
“Mañjuśrī! In what do you abide when you cultivate the perfection of wisdom?
“World-Honored One!”
“I cultivate the profound perfection of wisdom while abiding nowhere at all. “Mañjuśrī!
How can one who abides nowhere cultivate the profound perfection of wisdom?”
“World-Honored One!
It is because I have no abiding that I am able to cultivate the perfection of wisdom. “Mañjuśrī!”
"When you cultivate the perfection of wisdom, what is increased and what is decreased regarding the wholesome and the unwholesome?
"World-Honored One,
when I cultivate the profound perfection of wisdom, there is neither increase nor decrease regarding the wholesome or the unwholesome."
"Bhagavān!
As I cultivate the profound perfection of wisdom, there is neither increase nor decrease in any phenomena.
Bhagavān!"
The appearance of the *prajñāpāramitā* in the world is not for the sake of increasing or decreasing any phenomena.
World-Honored One!
Cultivating and studying the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is not for the sake of abandoning the dharmas of ordinary beings, nor is it for the sake of grasping all Buddha-dharmas.
Why is this? World-Honored One,
the profound perfection of wisdom does not arise for the sake of abandoning dharmas or attaining dharmas.
One who practices and studies the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does so not for the sake of wearying of the faults of saṃsāra, nor for the sake of delighting in the merits of nirvāṇa. Why is this?
One who cultivates this Dharma does not perceive birth and death, much less feel weary of them!
They do not perceive nirvāṇa, much less take delight in it!
World-Honored One!
When practicing and studying the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not perceive any phenomena as inferior or superior, as loss or gain, or as something to be abandoned or grasped.
World-Honored One!
When one practices and studies the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not apprehend any dharma that can be increased or decreased. Why is this so?
The true dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases.
World-Honored One!
If one can practice in this manner, it is called the true cultivation and study of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If one cultivates the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) such that there is neither increase nor decrease regarding all phenomena, this is called truly training in the profound perfection of wisdom;
if one cultivates the perfection of wisdom such that there is neither arising nor ceasing regarding all phenomena, this is called truly training in the profound perfection of wisdom."
If, while practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one perceives neither increase nor decrease in any phenomena, this is called truly training in the profound perfection of wisdom;
if, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, one perceives neither arising nor ceasing in any phenomena, this is called truly training in the profound perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If one cultivates the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not engage in mental construction regarding any phenomena; whether many or few, there is no aspiration for them at all. Being without attachment to the object of aspiration, the act of aspiring, or the one who aspires, is called truly practicing and studying the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one cultivates the *prajñāpāramitā* and does not perceive any phenomena as beautiful or ugly, superior or inferior, this is called truly practicing and studying the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If sons of good family cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not perceive superiority or inferiority among all phenomena; that is to say, they do not see at all 'this is superior' or 'this is inferior. This is the true perfection of wisdom."
Why is this? Because true suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality are neither superior nor inferior.
To practice in this manner is called the genuine cultivation and study of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī,
“Are not the sublime dharmas of all Buddhas also supreme? Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!
Because the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas cannot be grasped, it cannot be said to be superior or inferior; has the Tathāgata not realized that all phenomena are empty?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"So it is, young man!"
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the emptiness of all phenomena, how can there be superiority or inferiority?
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent! It is so!”
"So it is! It is just as you have said, Mañjuśrī!"
"Is not the Buddha-dharma supreme? "It is so,
World-Honored One!"
Although all Buddha-dharmas are truly unsurpassed, within them no dharma can be apprehended; therefore, it cannot be said that the Buddha-dharmas are unsurpassed.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Sons of good family, if one practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not wish to maintain or uphold any of the Buddha-dharmas, nor does one wish to discipline the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

This is because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* neither seeks to increase nor to discipline any of the Buddha-dharmas or the dharmas of ordinary beings, for it is without conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena.
If one practices in this manner, it is called the true cultivation and study of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Blessed One,
when sons of good family cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not perceive any phenomena that can be conceptualized or discriminated."
“Mañjuśrī! Do you not contemplate the Buddha-dharma? “No, [I do not].”
“World-Honored One!
If I were to see any true Buddha-dharma that should be contemplated, I would indeed see it; however, I do not see any.
World-Honored One!”

The perfection of wisdom does not arise for the sake of discriminating among phenomena; that is to say, it does not discriminate between the phenomena of ordinary beings, the phenomena of śrāvakas, the phenomena of pratyekabuddhas, the phenomena of bodhisattvas, or the phenomena of tathāgatas.

Sons of good family who diligently practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā* find nothing at all among all phenomena and have nothing to express; that is to say, they do not speak of a distinct nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) for ordinary beings, nor do they speak of a nature of phenomena for *śrāvakas* up to and including Tathāgatas.
Why is this? Because the nature of all these phenomena is ultimately empty and invisible.
To practice in this manner is called the true cultivation and study of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One, when sons of good family diligently cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not form such thoughts:
'This is the realm of desire (kāmadhātu); this is the realm of form (rūpadhātu); this is the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu); this is the realm of cessation (nirodhadhātu).'"
Why is this? Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not perceive any dharma that can be extinguished.
To practice in this manner is called the true cultivation and study of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If one cultivates the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one does not regard all phenomena as either beneficial or harmful. Why is this? "
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not act to sustain all Buddha-dharmas, nor does it act to discard the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Why is this so?

Sons of good family, you should diligently cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*, neither desiring to realize nor desiring to destroy the phenomena of ordinary beings within the Buddha-dharma, because you have realized that the nature of all phenomena is equal.
"If one practices in this way, it is called the true cultivation and study of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Mañjuśrī!"
Excellent! Excellent!

You are now able to expound this profound Dharma, serving as a true seal of the Dharma for the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, and also as a great seal of the Dharma for those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who possess overweening pride, causing them to know as it truly is that what they previously attained was not the ultimate realization.

Mañjuśrī! If good men or good women, upon hearing this profound Dharma, do not sink in spirit nor feel alarm or fear, you should know that these persons have not planted roots of goodness under only one Buddha, nor even up to a thousand Buddhas; they must certainly have planted roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas before they were able to hear this most profound Prajñāpāramitā without their minds sinking or becoming alarmed or fearful.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī joined his palms in reverence and again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to further expound the profound Prajñāpāramitā; I only pray that you will grant me your permission!"
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī,
“If you wish to speak, speak as you please.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If, when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one neither attains that which can be dwelled upon among phenomena nor attains that which cannot be dwelled upon, one should know that this profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not abide by taking phenomena as its object.”
Why is this? Because all dharmas are without an object of perception (*ālambana*).
World-Honored One!
If one can practice in this way, it is called truly training in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, because one does not grasp at the characteristics of any phenomena.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!"

One should contemplate this profound *prajñāpāramitā* by not manifestly contemplating the nature or characteristics of phenomena; for if one does not even manifestly realize the qualities of a Buddha, how much less so the qualities of a bodhisattva!
One does not even realize the dharmas of a bodhisattva, much less those of a pratyekabuddha!
One does not even realize the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha, much less those of a śrāvaka!
One does not even realize the dharmas of a śrāvaka, much less those of an ordinary person!
Why is this? Because all dharmas are detached from their own nature and characteristics.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!"

By relying on the cultivation of such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding any phenomena; that is, one does not discriminate between the distinctions of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as being conceivable or inconceivable. It should be known that when the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practices *prajñāpāramitā*, they are entirely without conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

By relying on the cultivation of such profound prajñāpāramitā, one does not perceive within any phenomena that 'this is a Buddha-dharma' or 'this is not a Buddha-dharma,' nor that 'this is conceivable' or 'this is inconceivable,' because all phenomena possess the nature of non-differentiation."
If sentient beings are able to cultivate this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and contemplate all phenomena as being the Buddha-dharma because they accord with bodhi;

and if they contemplate all phenomena as inconceivable because they are ultimately empty—these sentient beings must have already drawn near to, made offerings to, and honored many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, having planted various roots of goodness, before they are able to practice *prajñāpāramitā* in such a manner.

"Furthermore, Blessed One, if sons or daughters of good family, upon hearing this teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, do not become despondent nor feel terrified, it should be known that they have in the past already drawn near to, made offerings to, and honored many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and have planted roots of goodness; only then can they be thus."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, one should contemplate this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way: if one can diligently cultivate it, then regarding all phenomena, one perceives neither defilement nor purity;
yet, although there is nothing perceived, one is able to diligently cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, with a mind free from weariness at all times."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If one cultivates such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one will have no perception of distinction among ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or the Buddha-dharma, because one realizes that all these phenomena are ultimately empty."
"If one can act in this way, it is called truly practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī,
"How many Buddhas have you already approached and made offerings to?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!
I have already approached and made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the mind and mental factors of a phantom-maker, because all phenomena are like illusions.”
“Mañjuśrī! Do you not seek after the Buddha-dharma?
“World-Honored One!”
"I do not now see any dharma that is not the Buddha-dharma;
what, then, is there to seek? "Mañjuśrī!
Have you already accomplished the Buddha-dharma?"
“World-Honored One!
Now I do not see any dharma that can be called ‘Buddha-dharma’;
what, then, could be accomplished? “Mañjuśrī!”
“Have you not attained the nature of non-attachment?
“World-Honored One!
I am now the very nature of non-attachment; how could the nature of non-attachment further attain non-attachment?”
“Mañjuśrī! Should you not sit upon the seat of enlightenment?
“World-Honored One!”
Even for the Buddhas, there is no sense of "sitting" upon the seat of enlightenment, much less for me!
Why is this? Because all phenomena take the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as their definitive measure; within the limit of reality, both the act of sitting and the sitter are unobtainable.
“Mañjuśrī! What is the synonym for ‘the limit of reality’ (bhūtakoṭi)?
“World-Honored One!”
"One should know that 'the limit of reality' (bhūtakoṭi) is a synonym for the 'false body' (prapañca-kāya). Mañjuśrī!
How can the false body be called the limit of reality?"
“World-Honored One!

The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) neither goes nor comes; it is neither true nor false. Neither the body nor the characteristics of a body can be apprehended, and the same is true for a false body. Therefore, the false body is itself the reality-limit.”
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If bodhisattvas, upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), do not sink in heart nor become terrified, these bodhisattvas are certain to advance toward enlightenment and shall no longer regress.”
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If bodhisattvas, upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom, do not sink in spirit nor become terrified, these bodhisattvas have already drawn near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.”
"Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have realized that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is free from all conceptual construction, just like great enlightenment (mahābodhi).
Mañjuśrī also addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If bodhisattvas, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, do not become despondent nor terrified, these bodhisattvas are worthy of receiving the offerings and respect of the world, just like the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
"Why is this? Because they have awakened to the true nature of all phenomena.
At that time, there was a woman named Nirālambanā who, with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:

“Bhagavān! If sentient beings, upon hearing this teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, do not become despondent nor feel terrified, these sentient beings do not take as their objects of cognition any of the dharmas of ordinary worldlings, nor the dharmas of śrāvakas, nor the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, nor the dharmas of bodhisattvas, nor the dharmas of tathāgatas.”
"Why is this? Because one realizes that all phenomena are utterly non-existent, such that both the subject and object of cognition are unattainable.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra and the others:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."

If good sons or good daughters, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, do not become despondent nor feel fear or terror, it should be known that these good sons and good daughters already abide on the stage of non-retrogression; they are certain to advance toward enlightenment and shall never again fall back.
Śāriputra and others!

If sentient beings, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, do not sink in spirit nor become terrified, but instead rejoice, have faith and delight, listen, receive, and uphold it, and further explain it to others without weariness of mind;
these sentient beings are able to act as truly vast and sublime donors, capable of bestowing all unsurpassed treasures, and are fully endowed with the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

These sentient beings are perfected in pure ethical discipline; they possess true pure ethical discipline and supreme pure ethical discipline, their merit of pure ethical discipline is entirely fulfilled, and they are endowed with the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

These sentient beings are perfected in patience; they possess true patience and supreme patience, their merit of patience is entirely fulfilled, and they are endowed with the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

These sentient beings are perfected in diligence; they possess true diligence and supreme diligence, their merit of diligence is entirely fulfilled, and they are endowed with the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

These sentient beings have perfected meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); they possess authentic concentration and superior concentration, their merits of concentration are all fully perfected, and they are endowed with the perfection of concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

These sentient beings have perfected wisdom (*prajñā*); they possess authentic wisdom and superior wisdom, their merits of wisdom are all fully perfected, and they are endowed with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

These sentient beings have accomplished authentic and superior loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and are also able to proclaim and reveal the profound perfection of wisdom to others.
The Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
“For what purpose do you wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Bhagavān! I do not even have a mind that dwells in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, much less would I wish to realize it.
I have no intention of seeking or pursuing enlightenment.”
"Why is this? Enlightenment is myself, and I am enlightenment; how, then, can one seek to proceed toward it?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent,
young man!”
"You are able to skillfully expound upon the points of profound meaning.
You have planted many roots of goodness under previous Buddhas, long ago made great vows, and are able to practice various pure brahmacaryas based on non-attainment."
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one were to have anything to be attained among all phenomena, one could rely on non-attainment to cultivate the pure brahmacarya.
Yet, I do not see at all any phenomenon that can be attained or even non-attained; how then can it be said that one can rely on non-attainment to cultivate the pure brahmacarya?"
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī:
“Do you now see my śrāvakas’ virtues? [Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have seen it!
The Buddha said, "O youth!"
"How do you see them?
"World-Honored One!

Now I see all the śrāvakas as neither ordinary beings nor noble ones, neither those in training nor those beyond training, neither visible nor invisible, neither seers nor non-seers, neither many nor few, neither small nor large, neither already tamed nor untamed. I see them in this way, yet without the notion of 'seeing'."
Then, Śāriputra asked him:
"Since you have such a view regarding the Śrāvaka vehicle, how then do you view the vehicle of the Perfectly Awakened One?"
“Venerable Sir!
At present, I do not see a bodhisattva, nor do I see the dharmas of a bodhisattva.

I do not see awakening (bodhi), nor do I see the dharmas that lead toward awakening. I do not see any practice leading toward awakening, nor do I see any dharma for realizing awakening, nor do I see anyone capable of realizing awakening.”
"I see the vehicle of the Perfectly Enlightened One in this way: that within it, there is nothing at all to be seen.
Then, Śāriputra asked him again:
"How, then, should you view the Tathāgata?"
“Venerable sir! Stop! Stop!”
"Do not engage in debate with the Tathāgata, the Great Elephant-King.
Mañjuśrī! As for what is called 'Buddha,' what is this metaphorical designation?"
"Now I ask the Venerable One:
regarding that which is called 'self,' what further designation applies to it?
Śāriputra replied:
"The term 'self' is merely a conventional designation; it is a synonym for emptiness.

"Venerable sir, you should know that the designation 'Buddha' is the very same as the designation 'self. Both the self and the Buddha are ultimately empty; they are merely conventional designations established in accordance with worldly usage."

The name "bodhi" is also a mere conventional designation; one cannot seek a real bodhi by searching for it within this [name]. The characteristic of bodhi is empty and cannot be expressed. Why is this?
Because both name and bodhi are empty.
Since names are empty, verbal expressions are also empty; one cannot use emptiness to indicate empty phenomena.
Since bodhi is empty, the Buddha is also empty; therefore, what is called "Buddha" is a mere conventional designation for emptiness.
"Furthermore, Venerable Sir! That which is called 'Buddha' neither comes nor goes, neither arises nor ceases;

it is nothing to be realized and nothing to be accomplished. It is without name and without mark, beyond conceptual differentiation; it is without speech and beyond expression, incapable of being indicated. It is known only through subtle wisdom within one's own internal realization. That is to say, the Tathāgatas awaken to the ultimate emptiness and stillness of all phenomena and realize Great Bodhi; yet, in conformity with the world, they provisionally establish names and thus are called 'Buddhas,' for they do not exist as substantial entities. This is because neither existence nor non-existence can be apprehended."
"Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the subtle and wondrous wisdom realized by the Tathāgata is called bodhi; because he has accomplished bodhi, he is called a Buddha.
Since bodhi is empty, the Buddha is also empty; therefore, the name 'Buddha' is a designation for emptiness."
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The profound Dharma spoken by Mañjuśrī is not something that can be understood by beginners.”
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying:

"That which I have spoken cannot be understood by mere beginners alone; even Arhats who have completed what was to be done cannot know it. There is no one capable of knowing that which I have spoken."

Why is this so? The characteristic of bodhi is not that which can be cognized by consciousness; it is without seeing and without hearing, without attainment and without thought, without arising and without ceasing; it cannot be explained or demonstrated, nor can it be heard or received.

Thus, the nature and characteristics of bodhi are empty and quiescent; even the great bodhisattvas are not yet able to know them, let alone those known and understood by the followers of the two vehicles!
Since the nature and characteristics of bodhi cannot even be apprehended, how could there be anyone who truly realizes bodhi?
Śāriputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! Does the Buddha not realize the dharma-realm?"
"No, Venerable Sir! Why is that? Because..."
The Buddha is the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm is the Buddha; the dharma-realm should not, in turn, realize the dharma-realm.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, all dharmas being empty are called the dharma-realm, and this very dharma-realm is called bodhi. Since both the dharma-realm and bodhi are devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics, it is for this reason that all dharmas are said to be empty.

All phenomena are empty; awakening and the dharma-realm are all the Buddha’s sphere, non-dual and undifferentiated. Because they are non-dual and undifferentiated, they cannot be fully known; because they cannot be fully known, they are beyond verbal expression. Because they are beyond verbal expression, it is impossible to designate them as conditioned or unconditioned, existent or non-existent, and so forth.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The nature of all phenomena is also non-dual and undifferentiated. Because it is non-dual and undifferentiated, it cannot be cognized; because it cannot be cognized, it is beyond verbal expression; and because it is beyond verbal expression, it cannot be conceptually designated."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely non-existent; it cannot be designated as being here or there, nor as this thing or that thing.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one commits an act of immediate retribution, you should know that one is simultaneously committing the inconceivable and the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi).
Why is this? Śāriputra!
The inconceivable and the five immediate transgressions are both identical to the nature of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), without any distinction.
Since there is no one who can create the limit of reality, therefore the immediate transgressions and the inconceivable cannot be created either.
By this principle, those who commit the immediate transgressions do not fall into hell, and those of inconceivable capacity do not attain birth in heaven;
those who commit the immediate transgressions do not sink into the cycle of birth and death for a long night, and those of inconceivable capacity do not ultimately realize nirvana.

Why is this? Śāriputra, the inconceivable and the five acts of immediate retribution both abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); their nature is without distinction. They are without arising and without cessation, without going and without coming; they are neither cause nor effect, neither good nor evil; they do not summon one to the evil realms, nor do they induce rebirth among gods or humans; they are neither the realization of nirvāṇa nor the sinking into saṃsāra.
Why is this? Because the true Dharma-realm is neither good nor evil, neither high nor low, and has no before or after.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
A bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense does not fall into hell; one who purely maintains the precepts does not attain birth in heaven.
A bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense does not sink into saṃsāra; one who purely maintains the precepts does not realize nirvāṇa.
A bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense is not to be reviled; one who purely maintains the precepts is not to be praised.
A bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense should not be treated with contempt, nor should one who purely maintains the precepts be treated with excessive reverence;
a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense should not be treated with hostility, nor should one who purely maintains the precepts be treated with undue conciliation;
a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense should not be shunned, nor should one who purely maintains the precepts be sought after for intimacy.
A bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense is not one who should be diminished; one who purely maintains the precepts is not one who should be increased.
A bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense is not one for whom offerings should not be made; one who purely maintains the precepts is not necessarily one for whom offerings must be made.
A bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense does not increase outflows; one who purely maintains the precepts does not diminish outflows.
A bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense is not necessarily impure, while one who purely upholds the precepts is not necessarily pure;
a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense does not lack pure faith, while one who purely upholds the precepts does not necessarily possess pure faith;
a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense is not unfit to receive offerings of pure faith, while one who purely upholds the precepts is not necessarily destined to receive offerings of pure faith.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
within the true dharma-realm, whether one upholds or transgresses, their nature is equal and without distinction.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Those who are ordinary worldlings are called 'harmonious,' while the bhikṣus whose outflows are exhausted are called 'disharmonious. Mañjuśrī!"
"By what meaning do you make such a statement?
"Venerable Sir!

An ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who is joined with the causes of birth is called 'conjoined' (saṃprayukta); since Arhats do not possess such a condition, they are called 'unconjoined' (asaṃprayukta)."
Based on this meaning, I have spoken thus:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
those who are ordinary worldlings are called 'those who have transcended fear,' while the bhikṣus whose outflows are exhausted are called 'those who have not transcended fear.'"
“Mañjuśrī! Based on what meaning do you speak thus?
“Venerable Sir!”

Ordinary worldlings do not give rise to fear toward things that are truly terrifying; thus they are called "those who have transcended fear. The Arhats, however, know that terrifying phenomena are in reality non-existent, and thus there is no fear to be transcended.
Based on this meaning, I speak thus:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
all ordinary beings attain the patience of non-extinction (*anirodha-kṣānti*), while the assembly of bodhisattvas attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*)."
“Mañjuśrī! Based on what meaning do you speak thus?
“Venerable Sir!”

Ordinary beings do not delight in quiescence, yet they are said to have attained the patience of non-extinction (*anirodha-kṣānti*); the assembly of bodhisattvas does not perceive the arising of phenomena, yet they are said to have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*).
It is based on this meaning that I speak thus.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Those who are ordinary worldlings are called 'tamed,' while the bhikṣus whose outflows are exhausted are called 'untamed. Mañjuśrī!"
“By what meaning do you make such a statement?
“Venerable sir!

Because ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) have not yet been tamed, they ought to be tamed; thus they are called ‘tamed. As for the Arhats, because their outflows (*āsrava*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*) are already exhausted and they no longer require taming, they are called ‘untamed.’”
Based on this meaning, I speak thus:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

those who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are called practitioners who transcend through the higher mind (*adhicitta*), whereas *bhikṣus* whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*) are called those with inferior minds who do not practice transcendence."
“Mañjuśrī! Based on what meaning do you speak thus?
“Venerable Sir!”

Ordinary beings have minds that are haughty and act contrary to the realm of reality (dharmadhātu); they are called those who practice with a superior mind through transcendence. Arhats, however, have minds that are humble and act in accordance with the realm of reality; they are called those whose minds are inferior and who do not practice through transcendence.
"It is based on this meaning that I have spoken thus.
At that time, Śāriputra praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent!"
“Excellent!
You have skillfully explained the meaning of the esoteric words for me. Mañjuśrī replied:
"So it is! So it is, Venerable One!"
I am not only able to decipher the meaning of these secret words; I am also a true Arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
Why is this? Because I have forever ceased to give rise to any desire for the [paths of] Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, I am called a true Arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
The Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
“Is there any cause or condition by which one could say that a bodhisattva, while seated upon the seat of awakening, does not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Mañjuśrī replied:

“World-Honored One, there are indeed causes and conditions by which one may say that a bodhisattva sits upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) yet does not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). This is because within enlightenment there is not even the slightest dharma that can be named ‘unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. However, the nature of true enlightenment is without differentiation; it is not something to be attained by sitting, nor is it abandoned by not sitting.”
"For this reason, it can be said that although a bodhisattva sits upon the seat of enlightenment, they do not realize enlightenment, because signless enlightenment cannot be realized.
Mañjuśrī further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Unsurpassed enlightenment is itself the five acts of immediate retribution; those five acts of immediate retribution are themselves this enlightenment."

Why is this so? Both enlightenment (*bodhi*) and the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) are merely conventional designations; they do not possess a truly existent nature of enlightenment. They cannot be realized, they cannot be cultivated, and they cannot be perceived directly; the same applies to those five immediate transgressions as well.

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is ultimately imperceptible; therein there is no awakening and no awakener, no seeing and no seer, no knowing and no knower, no conceptualization and no conceptualizer. This equality that is free from characteristics is called bodhi; the nature of the five acts of immediate retribution is likewise so.
"Therefore, this bodhi is not something that can be realized; to say that great bodhi can be realized, cultivated, or directly perceived is the arrogance of overweening pride.
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī, "Do you now consider me to be a Tathāgata?"
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
"Sugata! I do not consider the Buddha to be a truly real Tathāgata. Why is this? Because..."

Now, the Tathāgata realizes True Suchness (tathatā) through subtle and wondrous wisdom; yet both this wondrous wisdom and True Suchness are devoid of marks. That True Suchness is devoid of marks does not mean it is [a substantial] True Suchness, and the same applies to wondrous wisdom—it does not mean it is [a substantial] wondrous wisdom. Since there is neither wondrous wisdom nor True Suchness, the Tathāgata, too, is not a [substantial] reality.
Why is this? True Suchness (*tathatā*) and wondrous wisdom (*jñāna*) are merely provisional designations; the Tathāgata is likewise so. They are neither dual nor non-dual.

Therefore, wondrous wisdom, true suchness, and the Tathāgata possess only provisional names and lack a single substantial reality; thus, one does not say that the Buddha is a substantially real Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī,
"Do you harbor any doubt regarding the Tathāgata?
[Mañjuśrī replied,] "No!"
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Sugata!"
"Why is this? Because I observe that the Tathāgata is truly unattainable, neither arising nor ceasing; therefore, I have no doubts.
The Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
“Does the Tathāgata not appear in the world? “No,
World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata!

If it were the true dharma-realm that appeared in the world, one could say that the Tathāgata has appeared in the world; but since it is not the true dharma-realm that appears in the world, for this reason, the Tathāgata also does not appear."
“Mañjuśrī! Do you think that the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have entered parinirvāṇa?
“World-Honored One!”
"Is it not the case that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas share the same inconceivable characteristic of the single realm? "Mañjuśrī, it is so!"
So it is! It is as you have said.
All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, share the same inconceivable characteristic of a single realm.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does the Buddha, the World-Honored One, currently reside in the world?
The Buddha said:
"So be it! Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, were to remain dwelling in the world, then the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, would also remain dwelling in the world."
Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas share the same inconceivable characteristic of a single realm.
Since this inconceivable characteristic is without arising or ceasing, how could the Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa?
Therefore, World-Honored One!
If future Buddhas are to appear in the world, all Tathāgatas shall likewise appear;
if past Buddhas have already entered nirvana, all Tathāgatas have likewise attained parinirvāṇa.
If a present Buddha were to realize manifest enlightenment, then all Tathāgatas would likewise have to realize manifest enlightenment. Why is this?
Because within the inconceivable, there is no distinction among all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

However, the people of the world are deluded and attached to various conceptual proliferations, claiming that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has birth and cessation, and that he attains enlightenment.
The Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
"The Dharma you have spoken can only be understood by the Tathāgata, non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, and Great Arhats; others cannot know it."

Why is this? Only the Tathāgatas and those like them hear this profound Dharma and realize it as it truly is, neither praising nor disparaging it, because they know that mind and non-mind are both unattainable.
Why is this so? Because the nature of all phenomena is entirely equal; both mind and non-mind are unapprehendable, and for this reason, there is neither praise nor disparagement regarding phenomena.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Regarding this profound Dharma, who would praise it or disparage it?
The Buddha said:
“O youth! The mind of those foolish ordinary beings is not a mind of true nature; it is identical to the inconceivable mind-nature of the Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“Is the mind of foolish ordinary beings and the non-mind nature identical to the inconceivable mind-nature of the Buddha?
The Buddha told the youth Mañjuśrī: “It is so!”
So it is! It is just as you have said. Why is this?
“Because the Buddha, the minds of sentient beings, and all phenomena are entirely equal and inconceivable.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If the Buddha, the minds of sentient beings, and all phenomena are all equal and inconceivable;”
Now, for all the sages and worthies who seek nirvāṇa, would their diligent practice and arduous exertion not be in vain? Why is this so?
Because the nature of inconceivability and the nature of nirvāṇa are without distinction; what need is there to seek it further?

If anyone should say that there is a distinct characteristic between these dharmas of ordinary beings and these dharmas of noble ones, it should be known that such a person has never drawn near to a true and pure spiritual friend; by speaking thus, they cause sentient beings to cling to the duality of dharmas as different, thereby causing them to sink and drift in birth and death, unable to attain nirvana.
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī,
“Do you wish that the Tathāgata be the most supreme among all classes of sentient beings?
[Mañjuśrī replied,] “World-Honored One!”
"If there were truly existent sentient beings, I would wish for the Tathāgata to be supreme among them; however, such sentient beings are in fact unobtainable.
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī, "Do you wish for the Buddha to accomplish inconceivable dharmas?"
“World-Honored One!
If there were an inconceivable dharma that could truly be accomplished, I would wish for the Tathāgata to accomplish that dharma; however, no such thing exists.”
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī:
“Do you wish for the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma and discipline the assembly of disciples? [Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!”

If there is the teaching of the Dharma that tames the true suchness of the dharma-realm, I pray that the Tathāgata may teach the Dharma to tame his assembly of disciples; yet, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared in the world, he possesses no debt of gratitude toward sentient beings.

Why is this so? Because all classes of sentient beings abide in the undifferentiated *dharmadhātu* of true suchness (*tathatā*); within this realm, neither ordinary beings nor noble ones, neither the speaker nor the listener, can be apprehended.
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī,
“Do you wish that the Tathāgata be the unsurpassed true field of merit in this world?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!

If these fields of merit were substantially existent, I would also wish that the Buddhas were supreme among them; however, these fields of merit are truly unobtainable. Therefore, all Buddhas are neither fields of merit nor non-fields of merit, because the nature of merit, non-merit, and all dharmas is equal.”

However, that field in the world which can never be exhausted is what the world collectively calls the "unsurpassed field. Since the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, realize inexhaustible merit, they may be called the unsurpassed field of merit.

Furthermore, that field in the world which is unchanging is commonly spoken of by the world as the unsurpassed field; because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, realize unchanging merit, it may be called the unsurpassed field of merit.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that the fields of the world are inconceivable: the world collectively refers to them as the "unsurpassed field," for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, realize inconceivable merit; therefore, they may be called the unsurpassed field of merit.
"Although the field of merit of all Buddhas is truly unsurpassed, for those who plant merit therein, there is neither decrease nor increase.
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī:
"Based on what meaning do you speak thus?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The characteristics of the Buddha as a field of merit are inconceivable. If there are those who plant merit therein, they will immediately be able to realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as equal and penetrate that all phenomena neither decrease nor increase; therefore, the Buddha as a field of merit is supreme and unsurpassed.”
At that time, by the spiritual power and the Dharma-power of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the great earth shook and quaked six times.
Then, within the assembled multitude, there were sixteen billion great bhikṣus whose outflows were forever exhausted and whose minds attained liberation;

seven hundred bhikṣuṇīs, three thousand upāsakas, forty thousand upāsikās, and a host of desire-realm devas numbering sixty koṭi-nayutas, all became free from dust and defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye.
Then, Ānanda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason does this great earth now tremble in six ways?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Because Mañjuśrī has explained the characteristics of the field of merit and I have now ratified them, this auspicious omen has appeared."
"The Buddhas of the past also spoke of the characteristics of the field of merit at this very spot, causing the great earth to tremble; therefore, such a phenomenon manifests now.

*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 574, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two of the Seventh Mañjuśrī Section. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Mañjuśrī is inconceivable. Why is this?
Because the characteristics of the dharmas taught by Mañjuśrī are inconceivable.
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī, “What you have spoken is truly inconceivable; it is exactly as the Venerable Śāriputra has said.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Dharma I teach is neither expressible nor inconceivable, yet it is also neither inexpressible nor inconceivable. Why is this?

Because both the nature of the inconceivable and the nature of the conceivable are non-existent; there is only sound, and all sounds likewise possess neither an inexpressible nor a conceivable nature, for the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is transcendent.”
"One who speaks in this manner is said to be speaking of the inconceivable.
The Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
"Have you now entered the inconceivable samādhi?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
"World-Honored One,
I do not presently enter this samādhi."
Why is this? Because I do not perceive the nature of this samādhi as being different from myself, nor do I perceive any mind capable of conceptualizing either myself or this concentration.
Regarding the inconceivable samādhi, since neither the mind nor the non-mind can enter it, how can one say, "I have entered this concentration"?
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!"

In the past, when I first began to train, I had to apply deliberate attention (*manasikāra*) to manifest entry into this samādhi; it was not the case that at present I again apply deliberate attention to manifest entry into this concentration.

It is like a skilled archer who, when first learning the art of archery, must fix his mind on a coarse target before he can release an arrow; once he has practiced for a long time and achieved mastery, he can shoot even the tip of a hair, no longer needing to fix his mind on that coarse target, but simply releasing an arrow wherever he wishes to shoot and hitting the mark.

In the same way, when I first began training in this state of concentration, I had to first bind my mindfulness to the inconceivable before I could manifest entry into this concentration; through long practice and achievement, within this concentration I no longer bind my mind, but am able to abide therein spontaneously.
"Why is this? I have already attained mastery in all meditative concentrations; I enter and emerge from them spontaneously without further deliberate effort.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Observe this youth Mañjuśrī; he is not yet to be trusted. Why is this?
Within this samādhi, it appears as though he does not abide constantly; yet there is no other samādhi so subtle and tranquil as this."
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Venerable One,
do you know of any other meditative absorption that is as tranquil as this?"
Śāriputra said,
"Is there yet another meditative absorption of such tranquility? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Venerable sir!
If this were obtainable, one could say that other meditative absorptions are as tranquil as this;
however, it is not obtainable. Śāriputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! Is this samādhi also unattainable now?
"Venerable Sir!"
This concentration is truly unattainable. Why is this so?

Because regarding all concentrations, those that are conceivable have characteristics that can be apprehended, whereas those that are inconceivable have no characteristics that can be apprehended. Since this concentration is said to be inconceivable, it follows that it must truly be unattainable.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There is no sentient being who does not attain the inconceivable samādhi. Why is this so?

The mind-nature of all beings is entirely devoid of mind-nature; that which is devoid of mind-nature is precisely what is called the inconceivable samādhi. Therefore, there are no sentient beings who do not attain it.
The Buddha praised the youth Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

Mañjuśrī! In the presence of immeasurable Buddhas in the past, you have planted many roots of goodness and long ago made great vows; all the pure conduct you have cultivated is based on non-attainment, and all that you utter speaks of the realm of profound meaning.
“Mañjuśrī! Do you not, by abiding in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, expound the most profound meaning at all times?
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If I were to speak thus by dwelling in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, I would be dwelling in the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*) and dwelling in the notion of existence (*bhava-saṃjñā*). If I were to speak thus while dwelling in the notion of a self and the notion of existence, then the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would have a point of dwelling. If the profound *prajñāpāramitā* had a point of dwelling, then the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would likewise take the notion of a self and the notion of existence as its locus of dwelling. However, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is remote from these two notions and dwells in non-dwelling."

Just as all Buddhas abide in subtle, wondrous tranquility—abiding by way of being without arising, without activity, without movement, and without transition—so too does the profound *prajñāpāramitā* not abide in existent phenomena nor abide in non-existent phenomena; therefore, this abiding is inconceivable.

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not manifest with respect to any phenomena. It should be known that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is itself the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*); the inconceivable realm is itself the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); the dharma-realm is itself the realm of non-manifestation; it should be known that the realm of non-manifestation is itself the inconceivable realm; and it should be known that the inconceivable realm is itself the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

The profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the realm of the self (*ātma-dhātu*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*) are non-dual and without distinction. That which is non-dual and without distinction is the realm of phenomena; the realm of phenomena is the realm of non-manifestation. One should know that the realm of non-manifestation is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. One should know that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the inconceivable realm. One should know that the inconceivable realm is the realm of non-manifestation. One should know that the realm of non-manifestation is the realm of non-existence. One should know that the realm of non-existence is the realm of neither-arising-nor-ceasing. One should know that the realm of neither-arising-nor-ceasing is the inconceivable realm. The inconceivable realm is non-dual and without distinction from the realm of the Tathāgata, the realm of the self, and the realm of phenomena.
"Therefore, World-Honored One!
If one can thus practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, one no longer seeks to realize great bodhi. Why is this? "
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is itself awakening (*bodhi*). World-Honored One!

If one truly knows the realm of self (*ātma-dhātu*), one knows non-attachment; if one knows non-attachment, one knows the absence of dharmas (*dharma-abhāva*); if one knows the absence of dharmas, that is the Buddha-wisdom (*buddha-jñāna*). Buddha-wisdom is itself inconceivable wisdom (*acintya-jñāna*). It should be known that in Buddha-wisdom there are no dharmas to be known, which is termed "not knowing dharmas."

Why is this so? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this wisdom is utterly non-existent; how can a dharma that is non-existent function within the true realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)? Since the intrinsic nature of this wisdom is non-existent, it is without attachment.

If there is no attachment, its essence is not wisdom. If its essence is not wisdom, there is no objective sphere (*viṣaya*). If there is no objective sphere, there is nothing upon which to rely. If there is nothing upon which to rely, there is no abiding. If there is no abiding, there is no arising or ceasing. If there is no arising or ceasing, it cannot be apprehended. If it cannot be apprehended, there is no destination. Since there is no destination, this wisdom cannot produce any meritorious qualities, nor can it produce what is not meritorious.
Why is this so? It is because there is no deliberation regarding "I am performing meritorious deeds" or "I am performing non-meritorious deeds.

This wisdom free from deliberation is inconceivable; that which is inconceivable is precisely the Buddha-wisdom. Therefore, this wisdom neither grasps nor rejects any phenomena (*dharma*); it does not belong to the past, present, or future; it is neither previously arisen nor previously unarisen; it is without emergence or disappearance, and is neither eternal nor annihilated. Furthermore, there is no other wisdom that can be compared to this wisdom.
Therefore, this wisdom is inconceivable; like empty space, it is beyond comparison. It is neither "this" nor "that," neither beautiful nor ugly.
Since no other wisdom can be found that resembles it, this wisdom is neither equal nor unequal; for this reason, it is called the "wisdom of the unequally equal.
Furthermore, since no other wisdom can be found to confront it, this wisdom is neither confronted nor not confronted; for this reason, it is called the "wisdom of the unconfronted confrontation."
The Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
“Is such wondrous wisdom unshakable? Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!
Such a nature of wondrous wisdom is immovable.
It is like a goldsmith who smelts and refines the raw ore; once it has been refined to its purest state, it remains unshakable when weighed.”

This wisdom is likewise: long cultivated and brought to maturity, it is without effort and without realization, without arising and without exhaustion, without emergence and without disappearance, stable and immovable.
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī,
“Who is able to believe and understand such sublime wisdom? Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!

If one can practice non-action regarding the dharma of parinirvāṇa, and likewise practice non-action regarding the dharmas of saṃsāra; if one practices the cessation of the practice of satkāya, and practices immovability regarding the practice of parinirvāṇa.”
One does not abandon lust, hatred, and delusion, nor is it that one does not abandon them. Why is this?
Because these three poisons are by their very nature detached; they are neither exhausted nor inexhaustible.
"Regarding the phenomena of birth and death, they neither arise nor fall; regarding the various noble paths, they neither depart from them nor cultivate them.
They possess deep faith and understanding in this wisdom.
The Buddha praised the youth Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent! Excellent!
You have well explained this matter."
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In future ages, who will be able to believe in, understand, and practice the profound meaning and intent of this Dharma-Vinaya?"
The Buddha addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa:

"Among the assembly of bhikṣus here in this gathering, there will be those who, in future ages, will be able to give rise to faith and understanding regarding the profound meaning of this Dharma-Vinaya that has been taught, and will listen to, receive, practice, and study it; they will also be able to explain and propagate it for others."
Just as a great householder who has lost a priceless jewel is bound by suffering and distress in his heart, filled with sorrow and discontent, yet later, upon regaining it, leaps for joy;

so too it is with the assembly of bhikṣus and others in this gathering. Having heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and having practiced and studied it with faith and understanding, they later find themselves no longer hearing such a Dharma-gate being taught.
Bound by suffering and distress in their hearts, filled with sorrow and discontent, they all think thus:
"When shall we ever again hear such a profound Dharma?
Later, if they should hear this Dharma-gate, they will leap for joy and exultantly think:
"Now that I have heard such a sutra as this, it is as if I have seen the Buddha in person and have approached him to make offerings."
Just as when the embryo of a tree adorned with circular garlands first emerges, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven leap for joy, saying:
"Before long this tree will surely put forth blossoms and its fragrance will pervade the air; we shall gather there to sport."

The assembly of bhikṣus is likewise; upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should receive it with faith, practice it, and give rise to joy, for before long all the Buddha-dharmas will blossom forth.

“Kāśyapa, you should know that if, in a future age, a community of bhikṣus hears such profound *prajñāpāramitā* and, with faith and understanding, practices it without their minds becoming despondent, they must have already heard it in this very assembly. Receiving and upholding it with joy, they shall explain and disseminate it. You should know that such individuals, through hearing this Dharma, will experience great joy and exultation; by believing, accepting, and practicing it, they will before long bring all Buddha-dharmas to full bloom.”

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if there are those who receive, uphold, expound, and disseminate this sutra, you should know that all such success in their endeavors is brought about by the empowerment and protection of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
"Kāśyapa, you should know this!

If there are those who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receive and uphold it with joy, they have planted many roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas of the past; they have already heard it before, not just now!"

It is like a pearl-driller who suddenly encounters a priceless mani-jewel and feels great joy; one should know that such a person has seen this jewel before, and thus experiences joy, rather than seeing it for the first time now.

In this way, when bhikṣus of the future who deeply delight in hearing the true Dharma suddenly encounter the Prajñāpāramitā and joyfully hear, believe, accept, and practice it, you should know that such individuals have already heard this sūtra in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas in the past; it is not the case that they could act thus by hearing it for the first time at this present moment.

“Kāśyapa, you should know that if good sons and good daughters, upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā spoken by Mañjuśrī, rejoice and leap for joy, delighting in hearing it without weariness, and repeatedly and earnestly request its further exposition—these good sons and good daughters must have, in the past, heard the Prajñāpāramitā being taught by Mañjuśrī and received, upheld, believed, understood, and practiced it with joy; they must also have previously approached, made offerings to, and honored Mañjuśrī. It is for this reason that they are able to act in such a manner.”
For example, suppose there is a person who enters a city and sees everything within it—the groves, ponds, houses, people, and objects—without exception.

Later, when they arrive at another place, they hear others praising the excellent things found in that city; they feel deep joy and request them to describe those things again. If they hear the description once more, their joy redoubles, because they have already seen all of it in the past.

Thus, those sons and daughters of good family who, in the future, hear this Prajñāpāramitā spoken by Mañjuśrī and joyfully delight in hearing it without ever becoming weary, who earnestly and firmly entreat him to further explain its profound meaning, and who, having heard it, praise it and experience redoubled joy—it should be known that all such individuals have, in the past, already drawn near to Mañjuśrī, made offerings and paid him respect, and listened to and received this Dharma; therefore, they are now able to accomplish these things.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Tathāgata has well explained the various practices, characteristics, and signs of those sons of good family, both present and future, who hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and practice it with faith and understanding.”
The Buddha said, "It is so!
It is as you have said."
"I have already well explained their practice, characteristics, and signs.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If good sons of the present and future hear this profound Dharma regarding these practices, characteristics, and signs, they should know that these are not truly practices, characteristics, or signs. Since the Dharma heard is subtle and tranquil, and all practices, characteristics, and signs are unattainable, why does the Tathāgata speak in such a manner?"
“Have I well explained their conduct, characteristics, and signs?
The Buddha told the youth Mañjuśrī: “It is so!”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.

When good men of the present and future hear this profound Dharma regarding all formations, characteristics, and signs, they will realize that these are in truth not formations, characteristics, or signs; for because the Dharma they have heard is subtle and tranquil, formations, characteristics, and signs are all unapprehendable."

However, when they hear the teaching of the profound Dharma, they joyfully accept, believe, understand, and practice it; this is because they must have previously heard, joyfully accepted, and practiced it in the past. Thus, such conduct, characteristics, and conditions exist as conventional designations, but in the ultimate sense, no such thing exists.

Mañjuśrī, you should know that the clear elucidation of the profound Prajñāpāramitā is itself the clear elucidation of all Buddha-dharmas and the thorough penetration of the truly inconceivable reality.
Mañjuśrī! All the roots of goodness I accumulated while originally practicing the bodhisattva path were fully perfected only through the practice and study of the profound Prajñāpāramitā.

Those who wish to abide on the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva, and those who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, shall likewise achieve their goal by training in and practicing the profound perfection of wisdom.
“Mañjuśrī! If good sons or good daughters wish to accumulate the roots of goodness accumulated by bodhisattvas, they should study this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
Mañjuśrī! If good sons and good daughters wish to abide on the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva, they should study this profound perfection of wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! If sons or daughters of good family wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should study this profound perfection of wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! If good sons and good daughters wish to skillfully penetrate the mark of equality of all dharma-realms, they should study this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Mañjuśrī! If good sons or good daughters wish to thoroughly understand the equality of the mental activities of all sentient beings, they should study this profound perfection of wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! If sons or daughters of good family wish to swiftly realize all Buddha-dharmas, they should study this profound Prajñāpāramitā.

“Mañjuśrī! If good sons or good daughters wish to understand the secret meaning and intent of the Tathāgata’s teaching that he cannot manifest full awakening to all phenomena, they should study this profound Prajñāpāramitā.”
Why is this? Because neither the dharmas that are awakened to nor the one who awakens can be apprehended. Mañjuśrī!

If good sons, good daughters, and others wish to understand the secret meaning and intent of the Tathāgata’s teaching that he cannot fully realize all Buddha-dharmas, they should study this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because neither the Buddha-dharma that is realized nor the one who realizes it can be apprehended. Mañjuśrī!

If good sons or good daughters wish to understand the secret meaning of the Buddha’s teaching—that the Tathāgata cannot fail to be fully endowed with the marks, signs, and majestic deportment of one who has realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—they should study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Why is this? Because the marks, signs, and majestic deportment of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that is realized, as well as the one who realizes it, are all unapprehendable. Mañjuśrī!

If sons or daughters of good family wish to understand the secret meaning of the Buddha’s teaching—that the Tathāgata does not accomplish all meritorious qualities and cannot transform and guide all sentient beings—they should study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings transformed by merit and all Tathāgatas are unapprehendable. Mañjuśrī!
If sons or daughters of good family wish to attain unimpeded understanding regarding all phenomena, they should study this profound perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not perceive even the slightest reality in any phenomena—whether pure or defiled, arising or ceasing, and so forth.

Mañjuśrī! If good sons or good daughters and others wish to know that all dharmas possess neither the characteristics of the past, future, present, nor the unconditioned, they should study this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because the true dharma-realm is neither past, future, nor present, and is unconditioned; all phenomena enter into the true dharma-realm. "Mañjuśrī!
If sons or daughters of good family wish to attain freedom from doubt regarding all phenomena, they should study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Mañjuśrī! If good sons or good daughters wish to be able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects, and to do so without any attachment whatsoever therein, they should study this profound perfection of wisdom.

Mañjuśrī! If good sons or good daughters wish to attain a mind of loving-kindness that universally covers all, yet without the perception of sentient beings therein, they should study this profound Prajñāpāramitā.

Mañjuśrī! If good sons or good daughters wish to enter the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) together with the world without any contentious debate, and yet find nothing at all—neither the world nor any contentious debates—they should study this profound Prajñāpāramitā.

Mañjuśrī! If good sons or good daughters wish to thoroughly and completely penetrate the spheres of what is possible and what is impossible without any obstruction, they should study this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Mañjuśrī! If good men or good women and others wish to attain the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and other boundless Buddha-dharmas, they should study this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As I contemplate this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is signless and unconditioned;
it possesses no merits, is without arising or ceasing, has no power or capability, and is without going."
It has no coming, no entering, and no exiting; it is without loss and without gain;
it is without knowledge and without vision; it has no essence and no function; it is not a creator, nor can it cause dharmas to arise or cease;
it does not cause dharmas to be one or different; it is without formation and without destruction; it is not wisdom.
It is not an object; it is not the dharma of ordinary beings, nor the dharma of śrāvakas, nor the dharma of pratyekabuddhas, nor the dharma of bodhisattvas, nor the dharma of tathāgatas.

It is neither realization nor non-realization, neither attainment nor non-attainment, neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion; it does not enter saṃsāra, nor does it emerge from saṃsāra, nor does it enter nirvāṇa.
