It does not emerge from nirvāṇa; it neither accomplishes nor destroys any of the Buddha-dharmas;
regarding all phenomena, it is neither created nor uncreated, neither conceivable nor inconceivable, free from all discrimination, and transcending all conceptual proliferation.
“If this perfection of wisdom possesses no merit at all, why does the Tathāgata exhort sentient beings to apply themselves diligently to its cultivation?
The Buddha told the youth Mañjuśrī:
“What has been thus spoken is itself the true merit of the perfection of wisdom. Sons of good family who understand it in this way are said to be truly cultivating the profound perfection of wisdom.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to study the supreme samādhi of a bodhisattva, wishes to accomplish the supreme samādhi of a bodhisattva, and wishes to abide within such a samādhi so as to see all buddhas, know the names of those buddhas, and see the worlds of those buddhas; and if they wish to realize and expound the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas) without obstruction or hindrance, they should study this profound Prajñāpāramitā, applying themselves with diligence day and night without becoming weary."
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason is it called the 'profound Prajñāpāramitā'?
The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī:

“The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is without marks and without names; it is boundless and limitless; it has no place of refuge; it is not an object of discursive thought; it is neither sin nor merit; it is neither darkness nor light; it is equal to the pure void and the true *dharmadhātu*, such that its boundaries and quantities cannot be apprehended at all.”
For these and various other such reasons, it is therefore called the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta!..."

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the profound sphere of practice for all bodhisattvas; if bodhisattvas are able to practice within this sphere, they will be able to penetrate all objective realms. Such a sphere of practice is not the sphere of practice for any other vehicle.
"Why is this? Because such a sphere of activity is without name, without marks, and is not an object of conceptual discrimination; therefore, it is called a non-sphere of activity.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha again:
“What dharmas do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice so that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha told the youth Mañjuśrī:
“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a mind free from weariness, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to correctly practice the samādhi of the single-mark adornment, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by the samādhi called 'Adornment of the Single Characteristic'?
How do the bodhisattvas practice it?"
The Buddha told the youth Mañjuśrī:
"This samādhi is adorned by the characteristic of the dharma-realm; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi Adorned with the Single Characteristic.'"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to enter such a supreme samādhi, they must first hear, inquire about, and study the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and only then will they be able to enter this samādhi.

Mañjuśrī! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not move from the dharma-realm, knowing that the true dharma-realm should not be shaken, is inconceivable, and is beyond frivolous conceptualization, they are thus able to enter the samādhi of the adornment of the single characteristic.

Mañjuśrī! If good sons or good daughters and others wish to enter such a samādhi, they should dwell in a secluded place, free from all clamor and distraction. Sitting in the full lotus posture, they should not contemplate various signs. Desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, they should single-mindedly fix their attention upon one Tathāgata, carefully grasping his name and clearly visualizing his physical appearance, maintaining an upright body and facing him directly in whichever direction he resides.
To continuously maintain mindfulness of this one Tathāgata is itself to universally contemplate all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Why is this so? Mañjuśrī!

The immeasurable and boundless merits, eloquence, and so forth of a single Buddha are equal to those of all Buddhas; for the Buddhas of the three periods of time realize Great Bodhi through the same True Suchness (tathatā) without distinction.

“Mañjuśrī! If good men or good women diligently practice and study until they attain entry into this samādhi of the single characteristic adornment, they will be able to universally comprehend the non-differentiated nature of the dharma-realm of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Furthermore, they will be able to maintain in their memory the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma already turned and yet to be turned by immeasurable and countless Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”

Although Ānanda possesses great learning and wisdom, having attained the dhāraṇī of mindfulness regarding all the Buddha's teachings, and is thus the most eminent among the assembly of śrāvakas, the teachings he upholds still have their limits.

If one attains such a samādhi adorned with a single characteristic, their vast learning, wisdom, mindfulness, and power of dhāraṇī will be inconceivable; they will be universally able to receive and uphold the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of immeasurable and incalculable Gaṅgā rivers, and will be able to thoroughly comprehend the profound meanings and purports of each and every dharma-gate, proclaiming and elucidating them with inexhaustible eloquence—surpassing Ānanda by many hundreds of thousands of times.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that those sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, upon attaining this samādhi, immediately obtain the boundless merit and benefits?"
The Buddha said: “Young man,
those sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who diligently practice and study the samādhi of the single-mark adornment constantly form this thought:”
"How shall I be able to universally penetrate the dharma-realm of all Buddhas, uphold all unsurpassed wheels of Dharma, and bring great benefit to all sentient beings?"
"By means of this, when one attains this samādhi, one immediately acquires boundless meritorious benefits. Mañjuśrī!

Those sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who first hear of the merits of this 'Samādhi Adorned with a Single Characteristic' will arouse diligent vigor and focus their mindfulness upon it in contemplation. In accordance with how they contemplate the merits of this concentration, so too will the characteristics of those merits manifest."

Having seen these signs as previously described, he gives rise to profound joy and applies himself even more diligently to practice; gradually, he enters this samādhi, whose meritorious benefits are inconceivable.
“Mañjuśrī! If there are sentient beings who slander the true Dharma, do not believe in good or evil, and possess heavy karmic obstructions, they will be unable to realize this samādhi.”
For example, suppose a person were to obtain a precious gem and show it to a gem-cutter, saying:

"This gem of mine is worth an immeasurable amount, yet its color and form are not yet very bright or fresh. You should polish and refine it for me according to the proper method, ensuring only that it becomes clear and pure without damaging its color or form."

The gem-cutter, following those instructions, polishes and refines it with focused mind according to the Dharma; as he does so, its luster and color gradually emerge, until finally it becomes transparent throughout from surface to core. Once thus refined, its value is immeasurable.

Mañjuśrī! It is likewise for those sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who gradually train in this samādhi; until they attain this samādhi, they shall obtain boundless meritorious benefits and virtues.

Mañjuśrī! Just as the solar orb universally radiates light to bring about great benefit, so too, when one attains the samādhi of the "Adornment of a Single Characteristic," it universally illumines the dharma-realm and enables the thorough penetration of all dharma-gates, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings; its meritorious benefits are inconceivable.

“Mañjuśrī! As I have taught, all various Dharma-gates are of one and the same flavor—namely, the flavor of detachment, the flavor of liberation, and the flavor of cessation—and they are without any contradiction.”

When those sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle attain such a samādhi, the Dharma-gates they expound likewise possess a single flavor—namely, the flavor of detachment, the flavor of liberation, and the flavor of cessation—and are without any contradiction.

When those sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle attain such a samādhi, they will possess inexhaustible eloquence in expounding the Dharma gates according to their exposition, and they will swiftly be able to bring the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) to full completion.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to correctly practice the samādhi of the single-mark adornment, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the various distinctions within the dharmadhātu nor its single characteristic, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

If sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle endure that the Dharma of a bodhisattva should not be practiced and that one should not seek to attain great enlightenment—because they have realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty—then by means of this endurance, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle believe that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma, and upon hearing that all things are empty, their minds are not startled or doubtful, then by virtue of this cause, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle hear it said that all phenomena are entirely empty, their minds are neither bewildered nor distressed, nor do they harbor any doubt; they shall never abandon the Buddha-dharma and will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, having heard these words, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas necessarily realized through causes and conditions?”
The Buddha said,
"It is not so. Mañjuśrī spoke again to the Buddha:
“Is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas not realized through causes and conditions?
The Buddha said, “It is not so!”

Why is this so? Because the inconceivable realm cannot be realized through causes and conditions, nor through that which is not causes and conditions; one should know that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is itself the inconceivable realm.

“Mañjuśrī! If sons or daughters of good family, upon hearing such a teaching, do not become terrified or afraid, I declare that they have already made great vows and planted manifold roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas.

Therefore, monks and nuns who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* taught in this way, do not become terrified, doubtful, or bewildered—they are those who have truly gone forth as followers of the Buddha.”

If laymen or laywomen, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, do not become startled, doubtful, or bewildered, they have truly taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
If sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle do not study this profound perfection of wisdom, they cannot be called those who truly train in the bodhisattva vehicle.
Mañjuśrī! Just as all the grasses,
trees, forests, medicinal herbs, and seeds in the world grow depending upon the great earth,
so too do all the mundane and supramundane roots of goodness, as well as other superior qualities, of a bodhisattva grow depending upon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

One should know that all phenomena embraced by this profound *prajñāpāramitā* accord with and lead to the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, without any contradiction or conflict.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this Jambudvīpa, in the future age, in which cities, towns, or villages will the profound Prajñāpāramitā be expounded and revealed so that many people will have faith and accept it?"
The Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
“In this assembly, there are sons of good family who, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, have accepted it with faith, practiced it, and joyfully made this vow:
‘May we, in all future births wherever we may be born, always hear the *prajñāpāramitā*.’”

"In whatever place they may be born in the future, by the power of their past vows, there shall be the teaching and exposition of such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which many people will faithfully accept."

Mañjuśrī! If sons of good family, upon hearing the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, rejoice with exultation and receive it with deep faith, I say that such individuals have long cultivated roots of virtue; it is only by the power of their past vows that they are able to act in this way.
Mañjuśrī! If there are those who wish to hear and receive this profound Prajñāpāramitā, you should say to them:
"O sons of good family!..."
"Listen with an open mind and do not give rise to fear, doubt, or lack of faith, which would only increase your slander and revilement.

In this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, no dharma is manifested; that is to say, there is nothing manifested that can be found as arising or perishing, whether it be the dharmas of ordinary beings, the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of tathāgatas.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there should be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or others who come to me and ask:
'How does the Tathāgata proclaim the profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the assembly? "
I should answer:
"The Buddha has taught that all dharmas are characterized by the absence of conflict. Why is this so?"
There is no dharma whatsoever that can contend with a dharma, nor is there any sentient being capable of producing faith and understanding toward what the Buddha has taught.
Why is this? Because the various classes of sentient beings are entirely unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
I shall say to them:
'The Tathāgata constantly teaches that all dharmas are the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).'"

Why is this so? Because all phenomena are equal and are entirely subsumed within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); herein it is not said that Arhats and others are able to attain the supreme Dharma.
Why is this so? Because the dharmas realized by Arhats and others are indistinguishable in their characteristics from the dharmas of ordinary beings.
“Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
I shall say to them:
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha does not cause sentient beings to attain, are attaining, or will attain parinirvāṇa. Why is this?"
"Because all sentient beings are ultimately empty.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
good sons and others come to my place and ask me this question:"
"O Benevolent One, you have previously discussed with the Tathāgata the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; please explain it for us now, for we long to hear and receive it!
To them, I would say:

"If you wish to hear, do not give rise to a mind that listens, nor fix your attention exclusively upon it. You should instead give rise to a mind that is like an illusion or a magical transformation; only in this way can you understand what I say."
If you wish to hear my Dharma, you should give rise to this thought:
"The Dharma heard now is like the tracks of a bird in the sky, like the son of a barren woman.
Only in this way can you listen to what I say.
If you wish to hear my Dharma, do not give rise to dualistic thoughts.
Why is this? Because the Dharma I teach is free from dualistic thoughts.

You should now not destroy the notion of self, nor give rise to various views; you should have no expectations regarding the Buddha-dharma, and take no pleasure in shifting or moving within the dharmas of ordinary beings.
Why is this? Because the two dharmas are empty of characteristics, and thus there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
"World-Honored One!..."

Whenever anyone requests me to proclaim the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, I first instruct and advise them by sealing all phenomena with the seal of signlessness (*animitta-mudrā*), causing those who seek to listen to abandon the mind of grasping and attachment; only then do I expound for them the teachings corresponding to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha praised the youth Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, excellent!
You have skillfully explained the Dharma I have taught, as well as the skillful means."
"Mañjuśrī! If good men or good women wish to see the Tathāgata, and wish to draw near to the Buddha to make offerings and pay him respect, they should study this profound Prajñāpāramitā."
If any sentient beings wish to request the Buddhas to serve as their Great Teachers, they should study this profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
If any sentient beings wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or even if they do not wish to realize it, they should study this profound perfection of wisdom.
If sentient beings wish to attain skillfulness in all meditative concentrations, they should study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
If sentient beings wish to exercise mastery over the arising of all meditative concentrations, they should study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this so? All samādhis arise with mastery only when one knows that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, and are unconditioned and uncreated. Why is that?
Because they have realized that all phenomena are empty and are thus free from all obstructions.
If sentient beings wish to realize that all phenomena possess transcendence—that there is not a single phenomenon that lacks transcendence—they should study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
If sentient beings wish to realize that all phenomena are merely provisional designations and lack true reality, they should study this profound perfection of wisdom.

If one wishes to understand that although all classes of sentient beings may set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there is no one who actually attains enlightenment, nor is there anyone who falls back or perishes, they should study this profound perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are realized as being identical to bodhi.

If one wishes to thoroughly understand that all sentient beings practice the conduct of bodhi—such that there is no conduct not practiced and no falling back—one should study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Why is this so? Because awakening is the true nature of all phenomena; all sentient beings engage in these phenomena, and there is no one who abandons them. Since all conditioned formations are empty, there is no falling back or perishing.

If one wishes to thoroughly comprehend that the nature of all phenomena is itself awakening, and that all awakening is itself the dharma-realm—which is the limit of reality, and the limit of reality is emptiness—one should study this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a mind free from retreat or despondency.
“Mañjuśrī! The profound perfection of wisdom reveals the inconceivable activities of the Buddhas that benefit sentient beings; it is also the sphere of the Tathāgatas’ playful mastery.”
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be demonstrated and cannot be expounded; it is a dharma that does not fall [into extremes].
Only the Tathāgata, having realized it as it truly is, teaches it to sentient beings through skillful means.

“Mañjuśrī! If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others who, regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, at the very least receive and uphold a single four-line verse and expound it for others, they will certainly proceed toward Bodhi and abide in the realm of the Buddhas; how much more so those who are able to practice according to the teaching!”
"You should know that such a person will not fall into the evil destinies and will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Mañjuśrī!

If sentient beings, upon hearing this teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, do not become despondent, nor are they terrified, but instead receive it with joy and faith—you should know that these individuals will certainly realize all the dharmas of the Buddhas; they are approved by all Tathāgatas and permitted to be received as their disciples."
“Mañjuśrī! If good sons and good daughters, etc., believe in and accept the unsurpassed Dharma-seal of the Tathāgata—namely, the profound Prajñāpāramitā—they shall obtain immeasurable merit.”
This Dharma seal is protected by the mindfulness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and is guarded by all Arhats, Bodhisattvas, wise ones, and celestial deities.

If sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle are sealed by this seal, they will transcend all evil realms, as well as the stages of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and shall certainly realize unsurpassed bodhi.

Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with immeasurable sons of the gods from the Heaven of the Thirty-three, each took various kinds of celestial, exquisite flowers and fragrances—utpala flowers, kumuda flowers, padma flowers, puṇḍarīka flowers, sūkṣmasvara flowers, maṅgalasubhaga flowers, and sandalwood powder—and made offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, scattering them over the Tathāgata, Mañjuśrī, all the bodhisattvas, and the śrāvakas;
they further played various kinds of celestial music, singing praises of the sublime Dharma as an offering;
and they further made this vow:
"May we always hear such a profound Dharma-seal as this Prajñāpāramitā!
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, further made this vow:
"May all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa always hear the Prajñāpāramitā, joyfully receive and uphold it, and thereby accomplish the Buddha-dharma!"
"We, the hosts of devas, shall constantly protect them, ensuring that those who uphold [this teaching] encounter no obstacles.
You should know that it is through the majestic power of the devas that all sentient beings are able to hear, uphold, read, and recite [it] with little effort."
At that time, the Buddha praised Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"Lord of Devas!

Since you are now able to make such a vow, those who hear this and joyfully accept and uphold it will certainly be able to accomplish the teachings of all Buddhas and swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, will protect and sustain the Prajñāpāramitā so that it may long abide in the world for the benefit of all."
At that time, the Buddha immediately manifested great supernormal powers, causing all the mountains and the great earth of this trichiliocosm to tremble in six ways;
he further manifested a smile, emitting a great radiance that shone universally throughout the trichiliocosm.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This is precisely the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s supernormal power to protect and sustain the Prajñāpāramitā, so that it may long abide in the world for the benefit of beings.”
The Buddha said, "So it is!
It is just as you have said."
By my supernormal power, I shall protect and uphold this supreme Dharma-seal of the *prajñāpāramitā*, causing it to remain long in the world for the benefit of sentient beings.

After the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have preached the sublime Dharma, it is the natural law that they all manifest great supernormal powers to protect and uphold this teaching so that it may abide in the world, ensuring that the devas and māras cannot find an opportunity to harm it, that wicked people cannot slander or destroy it, and that all non-Buddhists are struck with deep fear.
"If there are those who diligently study this Dharma, no obstacles or difficulties shall remain unextinguished.

At that time, when the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, the entire assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, with Mañjuśrī as their leader, along with the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus and others, and the entire gathering including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Seventy-Five.
